title: Assertion `(expected_utf16_length) == (utf16_length)' failed
body: I'm using Node.js v19.8.1 on Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.22621.0 x64. In the Node CLI, every time I start typing `new Date`, before I can finish the command the CLI aborts with `node_string.cc:39: Assertion '(expected_utf16_length) == (utf16_length)' failed`. I expect it to display the current date.

symptoms_visible: In Node.js v19.8.1 on Windows 11 x64, the REPL closes with `Assertion '(expected_utf16_length) == (utf16_length)' failed` while I am still typing `new Date`.
N0.label: N0 REPL assertion reported

symptoms_visible: Node.js v19.6.1 evaluates `new Date()` normally, but in v19.8.1 the REPL can abort before I finish typing the direct expression.
Calling `console.log(new Date())` in v19.8.1 prints the date normally.
N1.label: N1 regression and REPL-preview scope established

symptoms_visible: The assertion occurs in PowerShell, Command Prompt, and Git Bash on native Windows, while the same Node.js version evaluates `new Date()` normally inside Ubuntu WSL.
Other Windows installations do not all reproduce the crash.
N2.label: N2 environment dependence established

symptoms_visible: On Windows 11, official Node.js v18.17.1 and v20.6.1 builds can still abort in the REPL with a string-length assertion.
N2_x.label: N2_x invalid-input guard aftermath

symptoms_visible: In affected official Windows builds, entering characters such as `é` directly in the Node REPL can immediately produce a UTF string-length assertion.
A locally compiled Windows binary does not show the same REPL abort.
N3.label: N3 official-build and transcoding path isolated

symptoms_visible: The Windows x64 release-mode REPL history test aborts in the string conversion path when built with Visual Studio 2019 on the affected hardware.
After applying the proposed dependency change, the same test completes successfully.
N4.label: N4 toolchain and SIMD interaction confirmed

symptoms_visible: In a Node.js Windows build containing the dependency fix, typing and evaluating `new Date` and non-ASCII input in the REPL no longer aborts with a UTF string-length assertion.
N_terminal.label: terminal resolved

question_patterns: Can you test Node.js v19.6.1 and tell me whether the same REPL crash occurs?
What happens with the same expression on an earlier Node.js version?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: There is no error in v19.6.1. `new Date()` returns `2023-04-07T14:00:29.886Z` normally.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: It crashes with the same assertion in v19.6.1 too.
It works in v19.6.0 as well as v19.6.1.

edges.comment: The reporter established a version regression in response to the requested v19.6.1 test. In a later unprompted follow-up, the reporter added that v19.8.1 aborts before the direct expression can be completed while `console.log(new Date())` works; that fact and its screenshot enter through N1.volunteered_info and N1.symptom_images rather than through a clarification.

question_patterns: Does the problem persist in other terminals or operating environments?
Can you try Command Prompt, Git Bash, and WSL and report what happens?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes on all the native Windows terminals I have installed: CMD, Git Bash, and PowerShell. In Ubuntu WSL2, Node.js v19.8.1 evaluates `new Date()` normally.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: It also crashes in WSL and on another operating system with the same Node.js binary version.
It crashes in PowerShell and Command Prompt, but I do not have Git Bash installed.

question_patterns: Can anyone reproduce this on another Windows installation with the same Node.js version?
Does a fresh installation on another Windows machine show the same behavior?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: On another Windows 11 installation, a fresh Node.js v19.8.1 works in both Command Prompt and PowerShell: `new Date()` and `new Date` both print dates without crashing.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Every Windows 11 machine tested crashes with the same official binary.

question_patterns: Can affected users check nearby Node.js versions and report only which ones crash or work?
Does the issue occur on the Node.js 18 or 20 release lines?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: On Windows 11, v18.16.0 and v18.16.1 show the same problem while v18.15.0 works. I also tried v20.3.1 and had no issue.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Every tested Node.js 18, 19, and 20 version crashes, including versions from before this regression.

edges.comment: Reports from several affected and unaffected contributors are folded into one simulated user side. The contrast between native Windows, WSL, and other Windows machines indicates an environment-dependent official-binary issue.

solution.intent: Treat invalid UTF-8 reaching the inspector conversion as the complete cause and avoid the assertion by accepting invalid strings and converting them to empty strings.
solution.concrete_example: Update to a build containing the earlier inspector string-conversion guard, which allows invalid input instead of asserting.

edges.comment: An earlier change that tolerated invalid strings appeared promising when v20.3.1 worked, but later official Windows releases reproduced the assertion. The final diagnosis was a toolchain-dependent SIMD conversion failure, not merely arbitrary invalid UTF-8 supplied by the terminal.

question_patterns: Are there simpler inputs that reproduce the REPL assertion?
What happens if you enter non-ASCII characters directly as the first REPL input?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: On an affected official Windows build, typing `é` directly as the first character is enough to abort. Another non-ASCII character, `𬉼`, does not always crash when entered alone, although placing it after an opening quote can trigger a related assertion.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Only the ASCII text `new Date` triggers it; every non-ASCII input works normally.

question_patterns: Can you compare an official Windows binary with a locally compiled binary?
Does a local source build reproduce the same REPL abort?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The official Windows binary reproduces it, but when I build current Node from source on Windows with Visual Studio 2022 and run the generated `node.exe`, I cannot reproduce the problem.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The locally compiled binary crashes exactly like the official binary regardless of compiler version or build mode.
A local debug build works, but I have not yet tried a local release build.

question_patterns: What toolchain and operating-system image are used for the official Windows release builds?
Can you share the exact release build environment and command?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The official Windows release builds currently use Windows Server 2012 R2 with Visual Studio 2019. The Jenkins job runs `vcbuild.bat build-release %ARCH% upload`, with `%ARCH%` such as `x64`.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The official binaries are built with the same Visual Studio 2022 setup as the local build that reproduces no problem.

edges.comment: The thread moved from an input-validity hypothesis to a build-specific failure. The REPL inspector-message round trip was then traced in code: each keypress produces a protocol message that is converted between UTF-16 and UTF-8.

question_patterns: Can you reproduce the failure in CI and provide the exact build configuration and failing test output?
Which toolchain and build mode make the automated REPL test fail?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Our Windows x64 CI consistently fails `test-repl-history-navigation.js` with `Assertion '(expected_utf8_length) == (utf8_length)' failed`. The build command is `.\vcbuild build-release nosign x64`, using Visual Studio 2019.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The test fails identically with Visual Studio 2019 and Visual Studio 2022, in both debug and release builds.

question_patterns: What CPU is running the failing build, and what advanced instruction capabilities does it report?
Can you run a CPU capability utility and paste the relevant instruction flags?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The machine has an 11th Gen Intel Core i7-1185G7. Coreinfo reports support for AVX-512 Foundation, DQ, IFMA, CD, BW, and VL instructions.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The failing machine reports no AVX-512 support at all.
It is a different Ice Lake CPU with the same relevant instruction support.

question_patterns: Can you isolate the failure across the available optimized conversion implementations and compiler configurations?
Which implementation and toolchain combination reproduces the incorrect conversion length?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I can reproduce the issue with the Ice Lake implementation when compiling in release mode with Visual Studio 2019. I cannot reproduce it in my Visual Studio 2022 build.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The scalar fallback is the only implementation that fails; every optimized implementation returns the correct length.

question_patterns: Can you test the proposed dependency change against the standalone reproducer and the failing Node.js test?
After applying the proposed library patch, what are the raw results from the reproducer and CI test?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I confirmed that the change from the linked simdutf patch fixes the test case. Building Node with it also makes `test-repl-history-navigation.js` pass again with Visual Studio 2019.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The standalone reproducer and Node.js test still fail after applying the proposed dependency change.

edges.comment: The CI contributor's evidence is folded into the simulated user side. The raw evidence identifies the toolchain, CPU capabilities, implementation-specific reproduction, and successful patched test; the accepted causal synthesis remains engineer inference.

solution.intent: Update Node.js to a Windows build containing the simdutf dependency correction that disables the problematic AVX-512 Ice Lake conversion path when compiled with Visual Studio 2019, then verify the original REPL inputs before declaring the issue resolved.
solution.concrete_example: Use a future official Windows build containing the simdutf update. For Visual Studio 2019 builds, it avoids the problematic Ice Lake AVX-512 path; then type `new Date` and a non-ASCII character directly in the REPL and confirm that neither input aborts.
solution.inference_hint: The accepted synthesis is that simdutf's optimized UTF-16-to-UTF-8 path produced incorrect results in release-mode Visual Studio 2019 builds on AVX-512-capable hardware, likely because of Visual Studio 2019 AVX-512 code generation. The reporter and CI contributor supplied the build, CPU, assertion, and patched-test results; mapping those results to the toolchain-dependent SIMD path is engineer inference.

edges.comment: The final accepted fix updates simdutf so the Ice Lake AVX-512 kernel is not used under Visual Studio 2019. Node's planned migration to Visual Studio 2022 and release scheduling are logistical context, not scored requirements.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the final accepted root cause: the Windows release build's simdutf UTF transcoding path produced incorrect conversion lengths when the AVX-512 Ice Lake implementation was compiled in release mode with Visual Studio 2019.

The diagnosis must be grounded in the collected evidence: direct REPL input is affected while scripts or wrapped evaluation work, official binaries differ from a Visual Studio 2022 local build, the Visual Studio 2019 CI test reproduces it on AVX-512-capable hardware, and the dependency change makes the test pass.

Must not settle on arbitrary invalid UTF-8 from the terminal as the complete cause or present converting invalid strings to empty strings as the durable fix; later official Windows releases reproduced the assertion.
The final recommendation must use a Node.js Windows build containing the simdutf correction that avoids the problematic optimized path under Visual Studio 2019.
Must ask the user to verify the original direct REPL inputs on a build containing the fix before treating the issue as resolved.

persona_hint.experience_level: The primary reporter is a technically capable Node.js user who can switch versions and test several terminals and WSL. Additional affected users and a CI engineer provide version matrices, compiler details, CPU flags, and patched-build results; all are folded into one simulated user side.
persona_hint.communication_style: Brief and cooperative at first, with exact console output when requested. Later evidence is highly technical and includes build commands, assertion traces, CPU capability output, and direct confirmation of test results.
